# Non-unique, untrue and non-actionable candidate classes

<!-- Generated by catalog/build_catalog.py from catalog/classes.json. Edit the JSON, not this file. -->

Version 0.2 (prototype, 2026-11-08). 103 classes in 16 families, plus 5 proposed additions. Tiers: 36 solved, 42 harder, 25 open.

Each class is something a testing tool can hand a person that is not a new, true, actionable finding. The catalog's rule: **a filter may lower a candidate's rank or change where it goes, but only an oracle may close it.** Every trap below is a way a filter can hide a real finding; every re-test condition is what turns a label back into a question.

**How to read a row.**

- **Res.** (resolver): D = deterministic software (a fixed rule or diff); A = an agent with checks (bounded, logged probes against an oracle, re-verifiable by D or H); H = a person (business context, scope, risk ownership or ethics). Arrows show the usual escalation.
- **Tier:** solved = a known deterministic method exists; harder = the method needs statistics, an agent or a judgment threshold; open = no reliable method yet, or it needs a person. Panel picks carry the panel's tier; every other tier is this catalog's own assignment (inference).
- **Src:** Bracketed numbers are source keys. Each source was opened on 2026-11-08 and checked against the text of every class that cites it (catalog/CATALOG_SOURCE_CHECK.md). A dash means the class rests on reasoning, not on a source.
- **(P1) to (P7)** after an ID marks one of the seven panel picks; **(R)** marks a runner-up.

## The seven panel picks (ordered from solved to open)

| Pick | Name | Tier | Classes | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Soft 404s and catch-all 200s | solved | D1, D2, D3 |  |
| P2 | One finding, many addresses | solved | A1, A2, A3, B3 |  |
| P3 | The WAF answered, not the app | harder | C4 | Record it as 'blocked at edge, origin unknown'. |
| P4 | Works one time in N | harder | C7 | Pin each back end and report a success rate. |
| P5 | The target moved | open | O3, L2, A7 | Bind each finding to a target fingerprint at capture. |
| P6 | Our own footprints | open | B5, C5, C6, J4, L3 | Earlier runs, stored payloads, lockouts. Keep a shared side-effect ledger. |
| P7 | The agent grades its own work | open | T1, T2, T5, T6 | Provenance is solvable. Proving impact is still open outside crash, flag and browser-execution oracles. |

**Runners-up:** Callbacks from security products and CDNs (C10); Backported fixes (H1); Root-cause identity across tools (A8, B1); Honeypots that steer an agent (C8, F8).

## Family A. Same finding, many presentations (canonicalization)

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 (P2) | Redirects that converge on one origin | 301/302/307/308 chains ending at the same scheme, host, port, path and response fingerprint | D | solved | The hop can be the finding (open redirect; a cookie set without Secure before the redirect). Collapse findings about the destination, never about the hop. | Re-follow the chain; split again if the final origin or fingerprint differs. | - |
| A2 (P2) | Hostname aliases, CNAMEs and shared front doors | Same response fingerprint for the same path under different Host values; same certificate SAN set | D→A | solved | Grouping by IP or certificate merges different tenants on one CDN. Group by observed application behavior. | Re-probe each Host; split when fingerprints diverge. | [30] |
| A3 (P2) | Many IPs behind one load balancer (IPv4/IPv6, anycast twins) | Same banner, TLS key fingerprint and application response on N addresses | D | solved | Back ends behind one balancer can differ; one unpatched pool member is a distinct finding (C7). | Enumerate pool members; split any member that answers differently. | [43] |
| A4 | Wildcard DNS | Random-label probes resolve to the same answer as brute-forced names | D | solved | Explicit records coexist with the wildcard; a real vhost can share the wildcard's answer. | Re-probe surviving names over HTTP with the Host header before discarding. | [8] |
| A5 | Lexical URL variants | Case, trailing slash, percent-encoding, dot segments, default port, parameter order | D | solved | Equivalence is application-specific; cache-versus-origin normalization gaps are their own class (cache deception, path confusion). | Confirm equivalence by response, not by library normalization. | [35] |
| A6 | Versioned, localized and tenant-prefixed paths | Identical error signatures or stack frames under /v1, /v2, /en, /{tenant} | A | harder | Old API versions often keep weaker authorization. | Test each prefix; split where the result differs. | - |
| A7 (P5) | Mirrored environments (prod, stage, DR, blue/green) | Same build identifier and response fingerprint on N environments | D→H | open | A staging copy with real data or weaker authentication is its own finding. | Re-check build ID and configuration per environment at validation. | - |
| A8 (R) | One root cause, many sinks | Shared middleware, encoder, header policy or template marker behind many endpoint findings | A | harder | Same CWE is not same root cause; one sink may survive the global fix. | After the global fix, re-test every listed sink. | - |
| A9 | One vulnerable component across endpoints, images or hosts | Same component, version and advisory on N deployables | D | solved | Exploitability is per deployable; merging inherits the wrong reachability verdict. | Re-check reachability per deployable. | - |
| A10 | One misconfigured template stamped everywhere | Resource provenance traces to one IaC module, golden image, chart or CI template | A | harder | A local override can make one instance worse than the template. | Diff each instance against the template after the template fix. | - |
| A11 | Same control seen at different layers | One TLS terminator, WAF or identity provider in front of many apps | D→A | harder | An app that terminates TLS itself is a separate finding. | Confirm the terminating component per app. | - |
| A12 | Per-parameter explosion | Many parameters on one handler with identical behavior | D | solved | One parameter may reach a different sink (SQL rather than HTML). | Re-test listed parameters against the representative's oracle. | - |
| A13 | Many graph paths through one identity edge | Dozens of attack paths share one edge or ACE | D→H | harder | Paths that avoid the minimal cut are separate findings. | Recompute paths after the cut is removed. | - |

## Family B. Duplicates across tools, runs and testers

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 (R) | Cross-tool duplicates under different names | Different title, CWE or severity; same asset, root cause and location | D→A | harder | The earliest canonical record can hide a stronger instance; two tools agreeing on a title is not the same flaw. | Replay one tool's proof through the other's oracle. | [1] |
| B2 | Run-to-run drift | Hash changes from nonces, timestamps, session IDs or rotating markers | D | solved | A change in evidence can be a real change in behavior (a different error class). | Re-hash with volatile fields stripped; diff the error class. | - |
| B3 (P2) | Agent rediscovery across sessions | A renamed prior finding on the same asset | D | solved | As B1. | Retrieve prior findings for the asset before the agent proposes a new one. | - |
| B4 | Regressions masquerading as duplicates | 'Duplicate of closed #123' on a fixed item | D | solved | This is the over-suppression case: recurrence after a fix is new and high-signal. | Compare against fixed status on every match. | - |
| B5 (P6) | Tester-to-tester duplicates | Different people on the same scope and root cause | D | open | Another tester's stored payloads read as target behavior (contamination). | Claim lock on asset and root cause; check the shared side-effect ledger. | - |

## Family C. Artifacts of the test path, not the target

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | The tester's own proxy, VPN or tooling disclosing information | Header, error page or certificate text matches the tester's own tool | D | solved | The target may run the same proxy product; the proxy can mask a real header. | Diff with and without the proxy chain from a clean egress. | - |
| C2 | TLS interception on the tester's path | Certificate fingerprint differs from an uninspected vantage point | D | solved | An in-scope vendor TLS proxy in front of the target is a valid path finding. | Compare the certificate from a second vantage. | [7] |
| C3 | Egress filtering on either side | Silence on out-of-band checks; failed updates read as target errors | D | harder | Mostly false negatives: a missing callback reads as 'not vulnerable'. | Run an egress canary from both ends before trusting a negative. | - |
| C4 (P3) | A WAF, CDN or bot manager answering instead of the origin | cf-mitigated: challenge; vendor block page; text/html on a JSON API | D→A | harder | The edge blocks one payload while the origin stays open to another; the origin may be reachable directly. | Hold as 'blocked at edge, origin unknown'; re-test with an origin-side oracle, another encoding, or direct-to-origin in a lab. | [18], [19] |
| C5 (P6) | Rate limiting and throttling | 429, Retry-After, lockout pages | D | open | A missing rate limit on login is itself a finding; the test may have caused the lockout. | Back off; re-test at the original rate; record lockouts in the side-effect ledger. | [44] |
| C6 (P6) | Caches serving stale or shared content | CF-Cache-Status: HIT, X-Cache, Age | D | open | Cache artifacts can be the vulnerability (poisoning, deception); a test that poisoned the cache has real-user impact. | Replay with a cache buster; read Age and cache-status. | [32] |
| C7 (P4) | Load-balancer stickiness and heterogeneous back ends | Reproduces about 1 time in N; flaps between runs | A | harder | 'Not reproducible' is often one unpatched node. | Pin each pool member; report a success rate. | [43] |
| C8 (R) | Tarpits, honeypots and deception | Implausible port density, banners that change, a dormant privileged-looking account | D→H | open | A real service can hide among decoys; touching a honeytoken is an operational event, not a finding. | Person reviews before any interaction. | [11], [14], [45] |
| C9 | Captive portals and network login pages | Every host serves the same login page | D | solved | None noted. | Fetch a known canary URL before the run. | - |
| C10 (R) | Out-of-band interactions triggered by intermediaries | Callback source ASN is a CDN, IPS or mail scanner; late callbacks | A | harder | An intermediary that fetches attacker URLs may itself be an in-scope SSRF. Classify by source, do not drop. | Unique per-probe token and decoy; record source IP, ASN, user agent and path; host a file and see if the app consumes it. | [3], [24], [46] |
| C11 | The tester's own cloud or host context | Returned account or instance IDs belong to the tester | D | solved | Real SSRF to the target's metadata looks identical except whose identifiers return. | Compare from a second vantage point. | - |
| C12 | Lying or poisoned resolvers | Answers differ from trusted resolvers | D | solved | None noted. | Re-resolve with trusted resolvers. | [8] |

## Family D. Response semantics that fool detectors

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 (P1) | Soft 404s and catch-all 200s | 200 with an error page for any path; matches calibration probes | D | solved | A real resource whose size happens to match the error page. | Calibrate on several signals (size, words, lines, hash, title), not one. | [6] |
| D2 (P1) | SPA fallback routing | index.html for /.git/config, /.env, /backup.zip | D | solved | As D1. | Content type and body hash against a random path. | - |
| D3 (P1) | Protocols that return 200 on error (GraphQL, RPC envelopes) | 200 with an errors array | D | solved | Partial data plus errors can still leak fields. | Parse data versus errors; check data contents. | [27], [29] |
| D4 | The tool's own payload reflected back | Reflection in error, search or blocked pages, or JSON | D→A | harder | JSON reflection rendered as HTML elsewhere; a blocked page that echoes input can be XSS in the WAF's own page. | Require execution evidence (headless browser, print()). | [51] |
| D5 | Default virtual host | Unmatched Host routes to the port's default server | D | solved | The default vhost may be an unintended internal app. | Re-test with the correct Host; attribute by response. | [30], [52] |
| D6 | Intermediary error pages attributed to the origin | CDN, balancer or gateway 5xx fingerprints | D | solved | An origin stack trace wrapped inside a gateway page. | Fingerprint vendor pages; inspect the wrapped body. | - |
| D7 | Signature matches on generic content | root:x:0:0 or a SQL error string in docs or samples | D | solved | Low, if the control runs on the same endpoint at the same time. | Negative control: same request without the payload. | [51] |
| D8 | Dynamic-content diff noise | CSRF tokens, timestamps, ads, A/B buckets | D | solved | None noted. | Repeat the baseline; diff stable regions only. | - |

## Family E. Timing and nondeterminism

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | Network jitter | Latency variance swamps the effect | D | harder | Raising the threshold to kill noise also kills small real signals; report 'inconclusive', not 'no'. | Paired, interleaved samples; save the timing model with the finding. | [31] |
| E2 | Server-side noise | Load, co-tenants and interacting systems | D→A | harder | As E1. | As E1, with repeats spread over time. | [31] |
| E3 | Cold starts and scale-out | One isolated slow first response | D | solved | Cold starts sit near 1 s, where many SLEEP(1) probes sit. | Warm the target; discard first-request outliers; use larger, varied delays. | [33] |
| E4 | Blind time-based checks without a control | One slow response read as 'vulnerable' | D | harder | False positives usually appear once; a recurring one deserves a re-test. | Several delay values with dose-response, interleaved with zero-delay controls. | [23] |
| E5 | Timing detects 'something' else | A real timing difference with another cause | A→H | open | The signal is real but not the claimed behavior. | Test the claim from a second angle (content or out-of-band oracle). | [31] |
| E6 | Late out-of-band callbacks | Callback arrives after the scanner moved on (60 s polling) | D | solved | Time-window correlation attributes it to the wrong probe. | Correlate by unique per-probe token, not by time. | [3] |
| E7 | Model stochasticity (LLM targets and testers) | A one-time jailbreak, leak or 'safe' | D | harder | A low but non-zero success rate is still exploitable by an attacker who retries. | N trials; report the rate; fix temperature and keep seeds where possible. | [28] |

## Family F. Identity and context errors

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Wrong test user or role | Acting identity differs from the claim's identity | D | solved | None noted. | Record and assert the acting identity on every request. | - |
| F2 | Expired or invalid session | Mass 302s to login or login-page fingerprints | D | solved | An endpoint that really serves data without a session is the auth bypass. | Authenticated canary; compare with the authenticated body. | - |
| F3 | The test account's own data | 'IDOR' returns objects the tester owns | D→A | harder | None noted. | Two-account oracle: A creates, B reads; B reading its own object is the control. | - |
| F4 | Privileges or position a real attacker would not have | Allowlisted IP, internal vantage, WAF exemption, admin test credentials | H | open | 'Requires internal access' changes severity and route, not truth. It is a chain link. | Label preconditions; compare against the threat model. | - |
| F5 | Stale directory artifacts that look like privilege | adminCount=1 on an ex-admin | D | solved | The leftover non-inherited ACL is itself a hygiene finding. | Check current recursive membership, not adminCount. | [26] |
| F6 | Graph edges that are not exploitable | Contains edge where ACE inheritance is disabled | D→A | harder | The GPO path through the same container may still be valid. | Verify the effective ACE on the end object. | [42] |
| F7 | Point-in-time identity data | Path depends on a session that is gone (or appeared later) | D | solved | A gone session can recur on a schedule. | Timestamp session edges; re-collect before validation. | [41] |
| F8 (R) | Honeytoken and decoy identities | Dormant privileged-looking account with no logon history | H | open | Any sign-in alerts; never auto-interact. | Person reviews before interaction. | [11] |
| F9 | Theoretical versus effective permission (Kubernetes, cloud) | Static RBAC or policy analysis flags a binding | D | harder | can-i as an impersonating admin covers RBAC, not admission controllers or node paths. | Live effective-permission check, read-only. | [50] |
| F10 | Configured-but-not-live objects (certificate templates and similar) | Vulnerable in configuration, not enabled or published | D→A | harder | Anyone with rights on the CA can re-publish it. | Confirm publication and enrollment rights for a reachable principal. | [47] |

## Family G. True, but not the client's to fix, or not new

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | Vendor-hosted or SaaS components (in scope, different fix owner) | Real flaw on an in-scope URL whose fix belongs to a vendor | H | open | Most vendor findings have a customer-controlled half. Route both halves. | Re-test after the vendor advisory or the customer-side change. | [13] |
| G2 | Shared-responsibility layers and managed services | Control-plane or OS findings on a managed service | D | harder | Customer-specific and shared controls exist even on managed services. | Apply a service-to-responsibility matrix; suppress only the provider's half. | [12], [20] |
| G3 | Inherited platform defaults the customer cannot edit | 'Over-permissive policy' on a provider-managed policy | D→H | harder | Attaching a broad managed policy to a sensitive role is a customer finding. | Separate content (provider) from attachment (customer). | [38] |
| G4 | Intentionally public values | Publishable key types; system prompt text | D→A | harder | A genuine secret or guardrail sits next to the public identifier. | Suppress the identifier; test the control it relies on; inspect the payload around it. | [10], [25] |
| G5 | Known, accepted or compensated | Prior report, risk acceptance, VEX inline mitigation | D→H | harder | If the compensating control can be bypassed, the acceptance no longer applies: that is new. | Check acceptance expiry and conditions on every match. | [40] |
| G6 | Vendor and distro triage status | Distro 'negligible'; VEX not_affected | D | solved | Distro priority is not severity, and assumes typical use. | Keep suppressed items visible; re-check when use changes. | [9], [34] |
| G7 | 'Weakness, not vulnerability' findings | A risk-raising setting with no exploit on its own | A→H | open | Chains are made of these. Downgrade, don't delete. | Re-check when a chain could use it. | [37] |

## Family H. Version- and banner-based guesses

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H1 (R) | Backported fixes | Distro banner with an 'old' version | D→A | harder | Partial or reverted patches and pending reboots are real. | Credentialed package or OVAL query, or a behavioral probe for the specific flaw. | [2], [15], [17] |
| H2 | Modified, obfuscated or intermediary banners | Server header describes a proxy, or was removed | A | harder | Obfuscated means unknown, not safe. | Behavioral fingerprinting; confirm which hop answered. | [17], [48] |
| H3 | Version from leftover artifacts | CHANGELOG, readme or asset path shows a different version than the running code | A | harder | It can be wrong in either direction. | Behavioral probe for the specific CVE. | - |
| H4 | Manifest versus runtime mismatch (SCA) | Lockfile or scanned image is not what runs | D | solved | None noted. | Scan the running artifact by digest. | - |

## Family I. Reachability

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I1 | Vulnerable dependency never called | Call graph does not reach the vulnerable symbol | D | harder | Static reachability misses reflection, unsafe calls, dynamic dispatch and plugins. Unreachable means 'not shown reachable'. | Re-run reachability on each build; add a runtime probe where possible. | [4], [21] |
| I2 | Reachable path, harmless input | Path executes only with non-attacker input | A | harder | 'Harmless' sources change (a config value becomes user-editable). | Data-flow from an attacker-controlled source on each release. | [4], [40] |
| I3 | Component present, code absent or not executed (containers) | VEX component_not_present / not_in_execute_path | D | harder | A never-executed binary is still usable by an attacker with a shell. | Runtime evidence plus a signed VEX; re-check on image change. | [9], [40] |
| I4 | SAST source-to-sink with neutralization the tool does not model | Input replaced with static values before the sink | A | harder | A refactor can make the weak pattern live. | Path-sensitive data-flow or a dynamic test of the endpoint. | [39] |
| I5 | Dead code, feature flags, dev-only and debug paths | Code exists but is not deployed or enabled | A→H | open | Flags can be flipped by users or attackers. | Check deployment config and flag state on each release. | - |
| I6 | Network reachability | Vulnerable service bound to internal interfaces only | D→H | open | Internal-only plus an exposed SSRF is a chain. Re-rank, never drop. | Reachability matrix from each vantage point. | - |

## Family T. The tester is an agent (tool-side failure modes)

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap (how a filter hides a real finding) | Re-test when / how | Src |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 (P7) | Fabricated findings | Symbols, endpoints or parameters that do not exist in the target | D | open | Plausible prose costs expert time to disprove. | Every cited symbol must resolve; the claim must carry a harness-produced artifact. | [5], [49] |
| T2 (P7) | Evidence from the model, not the harness | Narrated responses with no captured artifact | D | open | As T1. | Harness hashes evidence at capture; the model may cite, not author. | - |
| T3 | The agent is prompt-injected by target content | Target pages or files carry instructions | D | harder | The injection itself may be a finding against the target's AI features. | Treat target content as data; run oracles independent of the agent. | [53] |
| T4 | Scope drift | Agent follows links into third-party or prohibited territory | D | solved | None noted. | Scope enforcement in the harness, not the prompt. | [13] |
| T5 (P7) | Severity and narrative inflation | Severity from prose rather than validated preconditions | D→H | open | Reports that read plausibly fool experienced maintainers. | Compute severity from validated preconditions and the impact oracle. | [5] |
| T6 (P7) | Non-reproducible 'success' | Success cannot be replayed | D | open | As E7. | Replay the recorded request sequence without the model in the loop. | - |

| ID | Class | Signal | Res. | Tier | Trap | Re-test when / how | Related |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| X1 | The target changed between scan and validation | Build ID, certificate or response fingerprint differs from capture | D | open | 'Fixed since' read as a false positive. | Re-baseline; re-run the oracle against the current target. (check_package: TARGET_CHANGED) | O3, L2, A7 |
| X2 | Stale or reassigned assets (cloud IP reuse, dangling DNS) | Ownership changed since the scope list was written | H | open | Testing someone else's asset: a scope and legal hazard. Belongs at the Scope check. | Re-confirm ownership before any probe. | O3 |
| X3 | Contamination from earlier runs or other testers' stored payloads | Payload markers that this run did not send | D→A | open | Our own residue read as target behavior. | Check the shared side-effect ledger; unique run markers. | B5, L3 |
| X4 | Effects the test itself causes (lockouts, rate limits) | Lockout or 429 that begins during the run | D | open | A test-caused state read as the target's normal behavior. | Record side effects; re-test after reset. | C5 |
| X5 | Staging and production mismatch | Validation ran on a different environment than capture | A→H | open | A result in one environment carried to another. | Bind the finding to an environment fingerprint. | A7 |

## Sources

Every source below was opened on 2026-11-08 and checked against the signal, trap and re-test text of each class that cites it. Keys a page did not support were removed, and a few pages were replaced with the primary or current page for the same point; catalog/CATALOG_SOURCE_CHECK.md records each decision. Most pages were downloaded and searched for the supporting wording; the pages that refused direct download were read through a fetch tool that returns quoted excerpts. Key numbers follow the research note the catalog was built from, so gaps mark dropped sources. 53 sources are cited; 43 of 103 classes rest on reasoning alone (Src -).
